title: The mathematical language of quantum science
markdown:
# The mathematical language of quantum science

*General graduate reference · original educational exposition · no project-specific data used as universal physics.*

## Learning goals

Develop the physical and mathematical background to derive a model, choose observables, test its limiting cases and recognise invalid numerical results. Prerequisites: complex numbers, linear algebra, calculus and SI units. See the [scholarly bibliography](../REFERENCES.md).

## 1. What a quantum state actually represents

In a complex Hilbert space the state |ψ⟩ is a unit vector up to a physically irrelevant common phase. For |ψ⟩=a|g⟩+b|e⟩, |a|²+|b|²=1 and measurement in the {|g⟩,|e⟩} basis produces probabilities |a|² and |b|². Complex amplitudes are not the same as the measured voltage from a detector. Relative phase changes interference in a rotated basis, while multiplying both amplitudes by e^{iφ} does not change an expectation value. One should distinguish a pure state, the state vector used to represent it, and a classical ensemble in which the same apparatus prepares different states on different runs.

## 2. Dirac notation and the Born rule

A ket |ψ⟩ is a column vector and its bra ⟨ψ| is the conjugate transpose. An inner product ⟨a|b⟩ describes overlap; it is generally complex. For a normalized projector P=|a⟩⟨a|, the probability of its outcome is ⟨ψ|P|ψ⟩=|⟨a|ψ⟩|². The identity resolution ∑_i |i⟩⟨i|=I holds for a *complete orthonormal* basis. It does not hold for an arbitrary set of nonorthogonal candidates. Real optical experiments acquire ensemble fluorescence or probe transmission, not single-state Born-rule outcomes directly. A forward optical model is needed between microscopic state and macroscopic data.

## 3. Basis rotations, phase and polarisation

A unitary U satisfies U†U=I; it transforms state coordinates as |ψ⟩new=U†|ψ⟩ and observables as Anew=U†AU. Expectations are unchanged, which is a valuable software regression test. For light or RF fields the Cartesian (x,y) basis and the spherical (π,σ±) basis are different coordinate descriptions of the same vector, with helicity sign determined by propagation and time convention. A phase error of π/2 can interchange a linear and circular basis inference. Write down the transformation explicitly before passing complex field components between optical Bloch, atomic-dipole and antenna codes.

## 4. Linear algebra for inverse science

The singular value decomposition A=UΣV† is defined for a rectangular matrix and reveals which parameter combinations are invisible or ill-conditioned. Rank identifies whether a noiseless solution can be unique; a small σmin controls amplification of some perturbations. A numerical condition number only has meaning after declaring units, column scaling and weighting. A transfer matrix mapping incident polarisation into an optical detector does not automatically become a quantum measurement operator. Distinguish the physical process from the numerical instrument-response linearization.

## 5. Calculus and coherent evolution

For a time-independent Hermitian Hamiltonian H the propagator is exp(−iHt/ℏ); its Taylor series involves matrix powers, not element-by-element exponentials. A diagonal Hamiltonian gives each energy eigencomponent a phase exp(−iEjt/ℏ), and interference depends on differences Ej−Ek. For a time-dependent H(t), a single exponential of its integral is invalid unless the Hamiltonians commute at different times. A numerical integrator should preserve norm in a genuinely closed system. Unit-normalised output can still be physically wrong if a time step misses rapid micromotion or if an angular frequency was supplied as cycles/s.

## 6. Statistics and uncertainty with real laboratory data

An average reduces independent, zero-mean noise, but it does not remove systematic calibration error. The sample standard deviation describes scatter; the standard error describes uncertainty of the estimated mean, and a naive 1/√N law fails for serially correlated laser scans. Covariance matters when the same frequency lock, temperature monitor or reference power affects several data channels. Record detector bandwidth and readout gains before comparing datasets. A photodetector output, atomic state variance and RF-field inference uncertainty are three different quantities.

## 7. Worked derivation and numerical checks

Let |ψ⟩=(|0⟩+i|1⟩)/√2. Measuring Z gives p(0)=p(1)=1/2. The Y-basis eigenstate |+y⟩=(|0⟩+i|1⟩)/√2 has overlap 1 and the opposite eigenstate has overlap zero, so ⟨σy⟩=1. Multiply |ψ⟩ by i and repeat: all probabilities stay unchanged. Now replace i with −i; Z-basis probabilities are still equal, but ⟨σy⟩=−1. Thus population measurements in a single basis cannot determine relative phase. Verify all calculations with explicit 2×2 Pauli matrices and complex conjugation in code.

## 8. Experiment-to-model checklist

Before a calculation: (1) state the physical observable and acquisition chain; (2) define your basis, signs and units; (3) write at least one analytically solvable limit; (4) test a change of coordinates; (5) check numerical conservation laws; (6) vary step size or discretisation; (7) record dependencies and raw inputs; (8) distinguish a simulation, measurement and algebraic illustration. These checks apply to virtually every Rydberg apparatus, from Stark spectroscopy to tweezer-array blockade.

## End-of-chapter questions and fully explained answers

### Problem 1. Why can no single-basis population measurement recover relative phase?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It squares amplitudes independently. Phase appears in interference terms once a noncommuting measurement basis mixes them.

</details>

### Problem 2. Which numerical method identifies weakly observable parameters in a six-by-four instrument matrix?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Singular-value decomposition, together with a declared noise metric and column scaling.

</details>

### Problem 3. What changes under a global phase e^{iφ}?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

State-vector representation changes but all density matrices and measurement probabilities remain unchanged.

</details>

### Problem 4. Why can a good-looking fit have an invalid uncertainty?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Errors may be correlated, the model may be biased, and fit residuals may violate the assumed likelihood.

</details>

### Problem 5. What is an essential unit check on a Hamiltonian?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

All matrix entries must represent the same physical quantity, typically joules or ℏ times angular frequency.

</details>

### Problem 6. Why do inverse-problem condition numbers depend on scaling?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Rescaling parameters or observations changes singular values and their ratio; dimensioned variables must be normalized meaningfully.

</details>

### Problem 7. What must hold for a closed-system numerical propagator?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It should be approximately unitary and preserve the norm of every input state, with errors controlled by a stated tolerance.

</details>

### Problem 8. How can one test a basis transform implementation?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Compute an observable in both frames and show numerical invariance of its expectation under consistent state and operator transformations.

</details>

## Advanced practical assignment

Implement a minimal self-contained version of the chapter's central equation. Supply its units, analytic limiting cases, a second independent check, and a reproducible test that fails when a sign or unit is changed. Distinguish generated illustrations from laboratory data. Explain how the model would be extended to a specific atomic species *only after* those foundations are correct.

## References

Use [F1] Foot, [Q1] Scully and Zubairy, [F2] Steck's Quantum and Atom Optics and the numerical analysis sources in [the bibliography](../REFERENCES.md). Consult original primary publications before reusing a parameter as experimental evidence.

# Operators, eigenstates and uncertainty

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Foundations · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

A Hermitian observable A has real eigenvalues and expectation ⟨A⟩=⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩. The variance is ⟨A²⟩−⟨A⟩². If A and B do not commute, ΔAΔB≥|⟨[A,B]⟩|/2. Spectral optical detection reads a response of an ensemble, not a direct projective measurement of a single Rydberg state. Measurement bandwidth and integration affect uncertainty but are distinct from a quantum uncertainty bound.

## Worked problem / research exercise

Represent σ_z as diag(1,−1). For |+x⟩=(|g⟩+|e⟩)/√2, predict 50:50 outcomes for σ_z, ⟨σ_z⟩=0 and variance 1.

## Lab / solver decision checklist

- Record relevant units, basis, frequency, coordinate frame and exact source version.
- Calculate the expected limiting-case behaviour before running expensive software.
- Keep the experimental or solver-native result separate from a numerical illustration.
- Test at least one independent reference, off-state or convergence criterion.

## Questions (attempt before opening the answer)

**Q. What is the distinction between a photodetector's electronic noise and intrinsic quantum state uncertainty?**

<details><summary>Reveal worked answer and explanation</summary>

Electronic noise is a property of a physical readout chain; quantum uncertainty describes incompatible observable statistics for a specified state. They need separate models and calibrations.

</details>

**Advanced discussion.** State the approximations used in the section, which observable could falsify the current explanation, and which source data you would need to validate a stronger claim. Compare this against the relevant source below.

Reporting an rms error in volts as an atomic density-matrix uncertainty; assuming quantum projection noise dominates without an experiment.

# Hamiltonians and rotating frames

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Foundations · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

The Schrödinger equation iℏ ∂t|ψ⟩=H|ψ⟩ maps energy to dynamics. For a two-level system under a coherent drive and rotating-wave approximation, H/ℏ=[[-Δ/2,Ω/2],[Ω*/2,Δ/2]] in a declared basis. Here Δ and Ω are angular frequencies (rad/s). If a library requests MHz instead, first check whether it means cycles/s or angular-frequency units. A frame transformation changes the representation, not the underlying experiment.

## Worked problem / research exercise

For a resonant drive Ω=2π×1 MHz, the ideal population Rabi cycle has period 2π/Ω=1 μs. Off resonance, Ωeff=√(Ω²+Δ²). Compare the slow drive, finite detuning and transit-broadening timescales.

title: Density matrices and open quantum systems
markdown:
# Density matrices and open quantum systems

*General graduate reference · original educational exposition · no project-specific data used as universal physics.*

## Learning goals

Develop the physical and mathematical background to derive a model, choose observables, test its limiting cases and recognise invalid numerical results. Prerequisites: complex numbers, linear algebra, calculus and SI units. See the [scholarly bibliography](../REFERENCES.md).

## 1. Ensembles and positivity

A density operator ρ=∑pk|ψk⟩⟨ψk| represents an ensemble. It obeys ρ=ρ†, Trρ=1 and ρ≥0. The spectral decomposition of a density matrix expresses it as nonnegative eigenvalue weights, but there can be many other ensemble decompositions of the same physical state. Pure states satisfy Trρ²=1; mixed states generally have lower purity. Populations are diagonal matrix elements in a specified basis and coherences are off-diagonal elements. A population-only rate model cannot generally describe phase-sensitive electromagnetically induced transparency.

## 2. Derivation of coherent density evolution

Differentiate ρ=|ψ⟩⟨ψ| and substitute iℏ∂t|ψ⟩=H|ψ⟩. The result is dρ/dt=−i[H,ρ]/ℏ, where [H,ρ]=Hρ−ρH. The commutator conserves trace and purity. An energy offset proportional to identity does not alter ρ, explaining why absolute energy reference drops out of isolated coherent dynamics. For an optical ladder, different laser couplings create coherences across the relevant states, and their interference can profoundly change probe absorption.

## 3. Lindblad dissipators without hand-waving

A Markovian completely positive master equation adds D[L]ρ=LρL†−(L†Lρ+ρL†L)/2. For spontaneous decay |e⟩→|g⟩ at population decay rate Γ, choose L=√Γ|g⟩⟨e|. Then excited population decays at Γ, while optical coherence typically acquires Γ/2 from that channel. Pure dephasing may suppress coherences without redistributing populations. Be careful about packages that express line widths as half-widths, full widths, angular frequency or cycles per second. A model can be numerically stable and still be physically wrong if dissipators are assigned to the wrong states.

## 4. Stationary solutions, uniqueness and trace constraints

Steady state solves Lρ=0 together with Trρ=1. The Liouvillian superoperator has a zero eigenvalue in a trace-preserving dynamics, but there can be multiple stationary states if the graph is disconnected or preserves a nontrivial invariant subspace. A solver must impose trace independently and should report the residual of the original equation. To check physicality, evaluate the minimum eigenvalue, Hermiticity error and trace error. Small negative eigenvalues may arise from numerical roundoff; larger violations signal an invalid model or numerical failure, not an invitation to clamp the solution silently.

## 5. From atomic coherence to optical transmission

The macroscopic polarisation at the probe frequency is proportional to atomic number density times a transition dipole expectation, often related to ρge. Susceptibility χ follows only after applying the correct dipole normalisation and optical frequency convention. Propagation through a medium depends on the complex refractive index; absorption and phase are distinct observables. A raw coherence plotted against laser detuning is *not* yet an oscilloscope voltage, nor does it include finite optical depth, cell windows, photodetection, beam geometry or servo drift. Distinguish susceptibility, normalised absorption, transmission fraction and calibrated volts in plot titles.

## 6. Thermal averaging and physical rates

A warm vapour contains atoms with velocity v distributed approximately by Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics. Each beam experiences Doppler shifts from k·v, with sign dictated by beam propagation, so a two-photon resonance retains residual Doppler sensitivity when wavelengths differ. Transit broadening depends on beam size and thermal velocity, blackbody transitions couple nearby Rydberg levels and can shorten effective lifetime, and collisions or optical pumping may introduce state-changing rates. Add each mechanism with a justified independent parameter, then perform velocity-grid and truncation convergence tests.

## 7. Worked matrix example

For ρ=[[0.7,0.2],[0.2,0.3]], trace is one, purity is 0.7²+0.3²+2×0.2²=0.66, and eigenvalues are approximately 0.7828 and 0.2172, hence physical. Completely dephase off-diagonal elements while preserving populations: ρ′=diag(0.7,0.3), purity falls to 0.58. A Z-basis measurement sees no change, while an X-basis measurement loses its original coherence-dependent bias. The example shows that incoherent ensembles with the same populations can have different spectroscopic responses.

## 8. A validation ladder for any optical Bloch code

Start with a two-level analytic limit. Add a third state and show the optical-coupling-off limit. Verify positivity, trace and residual at each detuning. Increase truncation until line shapes converge. For a thermal cell, double the Doppler quadrature resolution and report both the velocity span and convergence difference. When using a solver package, record its version, detuning units, decoherence conventions and exact state graph. Only after the physical observable is calibrated against independent data should a fitted RF field be described as a measurement.

## End-of-chapter questions and fully explained answers

### Problem 1. What are the basic physical conditions on ρ?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Hermiticity, positivity and unit trace. Purity is an additional diagnostic of whether a state is mixed.

</details>

### Problem 2. Why does a pure-dephasing jump alter EIT?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It damps coherence needed for interference, potentially destroying transparency even when level populations change little.

</details>

### Problem 3. How can a steady state fail to be unique?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Disconnected or symmetry-protected subspaces can support multiple stationary density matrices; inspect the Liouvillian nullspace.

</details>

### Problem 4. Why is Imρge not automatically equal to photodetector current?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

One must calculate susceptibility, propagate the optical field and include detector responsivity, amplification and calibration.

</details>

### Problem 5. How does a Doppler integral differ from adding a constant linewidth?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

It averages detuning-dependent responses over physical velocity classes, potentially yielding non-Lorentzian profiles.

</details>

### Problem 6. Why does coherence decay at Γ/2 in simple spontaneous emission?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

A population-decay jump attenuates the excited-state amplitude at half the population rate, yielding a Γ/2 optical-coherence damping contribution.

</details>

### Problem 7. What are minimum numerical checks for a solver?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Trace, Hermiticity, positivity, Liouvillian residual, convergence versus basis truncation and the relevant analytic limits.

</details>

### Problem 8. Why must the temperature be specified in a Rydberg lifetime calculation?

<details><summary>Reveal the solution</summary>

Blackbody-induced transitions and thermal populations depend on temperature, so an isolated radiative lifetime need not be the effective experiment lifetime.

</details>

## Advanced practical assignment

Implement a minimal self-contained version of the chapter's central equation. Supply its units, analytic limiting cases, a second independent check, and a reproducible test that fails when a sign or unit is changed. Distinguish generated illustrations from laboratory data. Explain how the model would be extended to a specific atomic species *only after* those foundations are correct.

## References

Use [F1] Foot, [Q1] Scully and Zubairy, [F2] Steck's Quantum and Atom Optics and the numerical analysis sources in [the bibliography](../REFERENCES.md). Consult original primary publications before reusing a parameter as experimental evidence.

# Angular momentum, fine structure and selection rules

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Atomic physics · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

Orbit ℓ, electron spin s and j=ℓ+s label alkali states; F=j+I adds nuclear spin and mF/mj labels projection. Electric-dipole selection typically requires parity change, Δℓ=±1 and Δm=q∈{−1,0,+1} relative to the chosen quantisation axis. q=0 is π and q=±1 are σ± spherical field components. The sign of a circularly polarised drive depends on the RF propagation and basis convention. A real EIT experiment may involve several coupled magnetic sublevels; one toy three-level ladder is not a full prediction of a Zeeman-sensitive spectrum.

## Worked problem / research exercise

Write a transition table for an illustrative j=1/2→j=3/2 pair at each allowed mj. Enumerate q values and reject endpoints that fall outside |mj|≤j. Recompute after rotating the quantisation axis.

## Lab / solver decision checklist

- Record relevant units, basis, frequency, coordinate frame and exact source version.
- Calculate the expected limiting-case behaviour before running expensive software.
- Keep the experimental or solver-native result separate from a numerical illustration.
- Test at least one independent reference, off-state or convergence criterion.

## Questions (attempt before opening the answer)

**Q. Why does changing the bias-field direction affect which RF polarisation component an atom sees?**

<details><summary>Reveal worked answer and explanation</summary>

The spherical basis is defined about the quantisation axis. Rotating that axis changes how a fixed laboratory RF vector decomposes into π, σ+ and σ− components.

</details>

**Advanced discussion.** State the approximations used in the section, which observable could falsify the current explanation, and which source data you would need to validate a stronger claim. Compare this against the relevant source below.

## Troubleshooting pitfall

Using arbitrary q to force a transition; treating π/σ as Cartesian x/y/z; assuming a field-alignment result without calibration.

# Rydberg quantum defects and scaling laws

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Atomic physics · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

For high-n alkali Rydberg levels, the energy relative to ionisation can be approximated E≈−hcR*/(n−δℓj)², where the quantum defect depends on angular state. Classical estimates give radius ∼(n*)²a0, adjacent transition energy ∼(n*)⁻³, polarizability often growing roughly ∼(n*)⁷ in suitable regimes, and radiative lifetime roughly ∼(n*)³ before blackbody/environment effects. These are scaling guides, not calibrated Rb-87 data. Use ARC's published level and lifetime APIs for numerical design.

## Worked problem / research exercise

At n*=70 and 90, the approximate adjacent spacing ratio ΔE90/ΔE70≈(70/90)³≈0.4705. Larger n yields smaller characteristic RF spacings. Check the actual chosen nℓj manifold with ARC before committing a laser wavelength.

## Lab / solver decision checklist

- Record relevant units, basis, frequency, coordinate frame and exact source version.
- Calculate the expected limiting-case behaviour before running expensive software.
- Keep the experimental or solver-native result separate from a numerical illustration.
- Test at least one independent reference, off-state or convergence criterion.

## Questions (attempt before opening the answer)

**Q. Why is hydrogenic energy E∝−1/n² insufficient for a high-accuracy rubidium transition search?**

<details><summary>Reveal worked answer and explanation</summary>

Alkali core penetration creates ℓ,j-dependent quantum defects, and fine/hyperfine interactions plus external fields affect precision. Use state-specific data.

</details>

**Advanced discussion.** State the approximations used in the section, which observable could falsify the current explanation, and which source data you would need to validate a stronger claim. Compare this against the relevant source below.

## Troubleshooting pitfall

Treating scaling laws as an HFSS result; assuming all ℓ states have identical quantum defects; ignoring blackbody lifetimes.

## Source and extension

# 780/480 nm rubidium EIT ladder

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Atomic receiver · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

The documented project uses approximately 780 nm probe light to drive Rb-87 5S→5P and approximately 480 nm coupling light to connect 5P to a Rydberg manifold. A specific nℓj transition is not fixed by quoting 480 nm alone: use measured wavelengths, detunings, polarisation selection and ARC-calculated transition access. Co- or counter-propagating beams have distinct two-photon Doppler behaviour. The photocurrent measures transmitted probe intensity, while EIT arises from driven atomic coherence; an RF field couples Rydberg levels and can alter the optical spectral structure.

## Worked problem / research exercise

Draw states |g⟩→|e⟩→|r⟩ and an RF link |r⟩↔|r'⟩. Label probe/coupling/RF Rabi frequencies, detunings and decay channels. Measure RF-off and coupling-off controls under identical detector gain.

- Keep the experimental or solver-native result separate from a numerical illustration.
- Test at least one independent reference, off-state or convergence criterion.

<details><summary>Reveal worked answer and explanation</summary>

# EIT dark states, absorption and Autler–Townes splitting

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Atomic receiver · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

In an ideal ladder with weak probe Ωp and coherent coupling Ωc, destructive interference can reduce probe absorption at two-photon resonance. The relevant observable is usually linked to the imaginary part of the probe coherence ρge, after susceptibility and propagation approximations. An RF drive between Rydberg states modifies the dressed eigenenergies; in the simple resonant strong-coupling limit the spectral splitting scales as ΩRF. A measured optical splitting is not generally ΩRF=2πΔf without accounting for propagation, projection and actual line-shape model. Thermal Doppler averaging and decay can merge or distort peaks.

## Worked problem / research exercise

Predict qualitatively how transmission changes if Ωc→0, if two-photon detuning moves off resonance, and if RF coupling grows. Run the documented RydIQule three-level benchmark before adding physical Rb-87 manifolds.

## Lab / solver decision checklist

- Record relevant units, basis, frequency, coordinate frame and exact source version.
- Calculate the expected limiting-case behaviour before running expensive software.
- Keep the experimental or solver-native result separate from a numerical illustration.
- Test at least one independent reference, off-state or convergence criterion.

## Questions (attempt before opening the answer)

**Q. Why can a weak RF field be present without two resolvable AT peaks?**

<details><summary>Reveal worked answer and explanation</summary>

Because the RF-induced splitting may be narrower than the effective homogeneous/Doppler linewidth and spectral resolution; fit the forward model rather than relying on peak counting.

</details>

Calling any two peaks an AT doublet; neglecting transit or optical-depth effects; using a resonant simple formula off resonance.

# Optical alignment, power and detection

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Laboratory · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

Laser alignment should begin with documented interlocks, beam paths, eyewear requirements and instrument reference settings. A photodetector's voltage is related to optical power via responsivity R(λ) and transimpedance gain; electronic bandwidth, saturation and offset must be checked. Optical density OD=−log10(T) and Beer–Lambert intensity T≈exp(−αL) are different expressions of the same attenuation when the assumptions hold. For an Rb vapour-cell EIT system, document laser locks, power drift, polarisation, temperature and probe coupling before changing RF geometry. Never infer line strength from a plot with uncalibrated vertical scaling.

## Worked problem / research exercise

For an illustrative diode with R=0.55 A/W and 10 µW detected, calculate 5.5 µA photocurrent. At 100 kΩ ideal transimpedance, the signal magnitude is 0.55 V before bandwidth, feedback stability and offset constraints.

## Lab / solver decision checklist

- Record relevant units, basis, frequency, coordinate frame and exact source version.
- Calculate the expected limiting-case behaviour before running expensive software.
- Keep the experimental or solver-native result separate from a numerical illustration.
- Test at least one independent reference, off-state or convergence criterion.

## Questions (attempt before opening the answer)

**Q. Why should detector bandwidth be recorded for Rydberg optical spectra?**

<details><summary>Reveal worked answer and explanation</summary>

A bandwidth limit filters transmitted intensity variations and may alter observed modulation/spectral scan dynamics; it is not interchangeable with RF carrier reception bandwidth.

</details>

markdown:
# Microwave fields, antennas and reference planes

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** RF engineering · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

In free space λ0=c/f and k=2π/λ0. At 1.925 GHz, λ0≈155.7 mm, comparable to many of the project's finite-board features. Poynting flux S=Re(E×H*)/2 for peak phasors; RMS and peak amplitude conventions differ by √2. Use calibrated dBm, cable losses and VNA reference planes; near-field coupling may not obey ideal far-field plane-wave assumptions. An antenna orientation sweep does not by itself establish a local E-field at the rubidium atoms.

## Worked problem / research exercise

At f=1.925 GHz, calculate λ0≈0.1557 m. A 70×50 mm receiving aperture spans about 0.45λ0×0.32λ0, which helps explain why a large periodic infinite-surface approximation can differ from a compact finite device.

# Jones vectors, Stokes coordinates and conventions

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Polarimetry · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

For a fully coherent transverse electric Jones vector E=[Ex,Ey]^T, define S0=|Ex|²+|Ey|², S1=|Ex|²−|Ey|², S2=2Re(Ex Ey*), S3=2Im(Ex Ey*) under one explicit time/handedness convention. This S3 sign is not universally shared; preserve the optical/radio convention along with the propagation direction. For an ideal pure input, S1²+S2²+S3²=S0²; partially polarised states lie inside the sphere. Linear analyser rotations alone sample S1,S2 but are insensitive to handedness S3.

## Worked problem / research exercise

Calculate Stokes for Ex=1/√2, Ey=i/√2. With the formula above, ExEy*=−i/2, so S3=−1. Reverse the relative phase and S3 flips. Verify that the project model uses its own stated convention when comparing handedness labels.

# Matrix rank, singular values and reconstruction

**Book:** Rydberg Systems Engineering · **Part:** Polarimetry · **Status:** original educational text, not new experimental evidence.

## Why this matters in our project

For y=AS+η with m≥4 analyzer states, A∈R^(m×4). Rank(A)=4 is necessary for a unique noiseless least-squares four-coordinate solution. The singular values determine numerical stability: κ2(A)=σmax/σmin, but row normalisation changes the condition measure. Weighted inversion is (AᵀWA)⁻¹ AᵀWy when full rank and assumptions hold. A physically valid Stokes estimate additionally obeys S0≥√(S1²+S2²+S3²) and S0≥0. A numerical test with input S and y=AS only validates the algebra, not the HFSS model or atomic receiver.

## Worked problem / research exercise

Take an orthonormal 4×4 A: κ=1. Repeat one row six times instead of adding independent responses: rank can fall below four, and full Stokes becomes unrecoverable. Compare this with the archived six-mask matrix and identify the smallest singular value after specifying row scaling.
